title: The Power of the Collection Habit
coreMove: Route every open loop — however trivial — into a capture tool at the moment it surfaces, before deciding what any of it means.

exampleSpecs.domain: a night-shift ER triage nurse mentally rehearsing unfinished handoffs during the elevator ride to the parking garage
exampleSpecs.audience: a mid-career ER nurse working 12-hour rotations
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a verbal medication follow-up mentioned by a departing colleague reaches the incoming shift or disappears with the elevator doors
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she stops rehearsing the list in her head and writes each item in her pocket notebook before stepping outside, recognizing that mental repetition is not capture — it is rehearsal that burns energy without moving anything to safety

exampleSpecs.domain: a freelance live-sound engineer driving home after a festival load-out, replaying a venue manager's offhand comment about rebooking next summer
exampleSpecs.audience: a self-employed audio technician in his late 20s with an irregular schedule
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a potential recurring contract disappears because he trusted a fatigued memory on a 45-minute drive
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the vignette ends the moment he pulls over and voice-memos three open items — not because the drive is risky, but because the car is not an inbox, and the mental loop has been running on repeat for 20 miles without resolving

exampleSpecs.domain: a high school orchestra director managing a budget meeting, a reed inventory shortage, and a parent complaint in the same afternoon
exampleSpecs.audience: a music teacher who doubles as department head at a mid-size public school
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a facilities work order for a broken music stand gets submitted before Thursday's concert or causes a student injury
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the 'before' shows her carrying four unwritten items through a two-hour rehearsal, her attention slipping to each in turn; the 'after' shows her writing each item on a capture list the moment it surfaces, so rehearsal gets her full attention and nothing depends on her remembering later

exampleSpecs.domain: a solo residential real-estate attorney explaining to a new associate why he writes everything down immediately, even items he is certain he will remember
exampleSpecs.audience: a practitioner in his mid-40s who developed the habit after a specific costly mistake
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the associate understands that a missed capture is a system failure, not a character flaw, and builds the habit before her first closing
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he names a specific incident — a document request he held in his head for 'just two minutes' that cost a client a closing date — and frames writing-it-down as transferring responsibility from a fallible organ to a reliable container, not an admission of weakness

exampleSpecs.domain: a sous chef conducting a Wednesday debrief after service collapsed: three verbal-only communications about a fish substitution that no one wrote down
exampleSpecs.audience: a sous chef in a mid-size restaurant who runs a weekly post-service debrief with line cooks
exampleSpecs.stakes: two wasted proteins, a comped table, and a line cook who feels unfairly blamed for a failure she was never clearly told about
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the debrief traces each failure back to the exact moment someone said 'I'll remember that' instead of writing it on the ticket or the station board — the problem was never skill or attention, it was capture discipline

exampleSpecs.domain: inviting the reader to spend 15 uninterrupted minutes writing down everything that currently has any claim on their attention, without stopping to process or prioritize any of it
exampleSpecs.audience: the reader directly, wherever they are reading
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether they discover that the weight they have been calling 'being busy' is mostly the friction of holding open loops in working memory rather than the size of the work itself
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after the sweep, the reader is asked how many of those items required action in the next five minutes — the expected answer is almost none — and the act of capture is shown to remove urgency without removing the commitment, which is exactly what the mind has been waiting for permission to do
